title: ר' יוסי בן קסמא

paragraphs: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma, end of Avot, chapter 6. In Chelek 98 his students asked him: ‘When will David’s son come?’ He replied: ‘Provided you do not ask for a sign.’ They said: ‘We shall not ask for a sign.’ He replied: ‘When this gate falls’—Rashi explains, of Aram; it should read Rome, for he was in Aram at that moment—‘and is rebuilt, falls and is rebuilt, falls and is not rebuilt again,’ and so forth. They told him: ‘Give us a sign.’ He replied: ‘Did you not say that you would not ask for a sign?’ They said: ‘Nevertheless.’ He replied: ‘If so, let the water of the cave of Pamyas turn to blood,’ and it turned. At his departure he told them: ‘Set my coffin deep’—in the earth, as Rashi explains—‘for there is no coffin in the Land of Israel from which a Median horse will not eat straw.’ Rashi explains: in the war of Gog and Magog. Chiddushei Aggadot writes: ‘When this gate falls’—see Rashi, who took care to explain this as Aram’s gate, meaning Rome, for the gate’s falling twice is a sign of Aram’s downfall, mentioned in several scriptural passages. Yet the subsequent passage appears to show that Rabbi Yose ben Kisma lived in the Land of Israel, for at his departure he said: ‘Set my coffin deep, for there is no coffin in the Land of Israel,’ and so forth. In Shanu Chakhamim Rabbi Yose ben Kisma said: ‘I am from a great city of sages.’ This implies that he was not in Aram. End quotation. One could say that Rashi was therefore precise: ‘He was in Aram at that moment.’ He intended to answer Chiddushei Aggadot’s question: he lived in the Land of Israel; therefore Rashi wrote ‘at that moment he was in Aram.’ One may answer that Chiddushei Aggadot well understood that Rashi specified ‘at that moment he was in Aram’ because Rabbi Yose ben Kisma said ‘when this gate falls,’ as though pointing with his finger; this compelled Rashi to explain that he was there then. But Chiddushei Aggadot refuses this, because ‘this’ does not so necessarily mean he saw the gate and pointed at it. ‘This’ applies to something famous and known even when it is not before him. Thus in Yitro, ‘On this day they came to the wilderness of Sinai’ means ‘on that day.’ Likewise in Vaetchannan: ‘Let me cross over and see this good mountain,’ meaning Jerusalem; yet Moses did not see Jerusalem, being far away, and said ‘this’ as though pointing with his finger. Likewise Psalms, section 74: ‘Mount Zion, this wherein You dwelt,’ and many such cases, as ‘For this man Moses.’ Rabbenu Bachya, Bechukkotai, writes: ‘This’ applies to someone of whom one has knowledge and whom one clearly recognizes. ‘This’ need not be understood literally of something standing before a person; it is like ‘For this man Moses’ in Exodus 32: they already knew him, though he did not stand with them. End quotation. Since it is known that the Messiah sits at Aram’s gate, as we shall mention below, he said ‘this gate.’ Thus there is no necessity that he was there then. Concerning this Chiddushei Aggadot wrote that he lived in the Land of Israel. But my heart does not judge thus. Rashi’s ‘He was in Aram at that moment’ was not derived from ‘when this gate falls’ as though pointing. Rashi did not overlook that ‘this’ may refer to something not before him. Rather, Rashi’s proof that he was in Aram at that moment was Avodah Zarah 18a: when Rabbi Yose ben Kisma became ill, Rabbi Chananyah ben Teradyon went to visit him. Rabbi Yose ben Kisma told him: ‘Chananyah, my son, Heaven has given this nation kingship and success, for it destroyed our God’s house. Yet you sit gathering public assemblies, with a Torah scroll in your lap. I wonder whether they will not burn you and the Torah scroll,’ and so forth. Not many days passed before Rabbi Yose ben Kisma died. All Rome’s great men went to bury him and deliver a great eulogy. On their return they found Rabbi Chananyah ben Teradyon assembling gatherings with a Torah scroll in his lap. They surrounded him with bundles of branches and burned him and his Torah scroll, and so forth. They placed his daughter in a brothel, and so forth. Rabbi Meir’s wife too was Rabbi Chananyah ben Teradyon’s daughter. Rabbi Meir went to rescue his aforementioned sister-in-law from the brothel in Rome. The matter became known; Rabbi Meir fled, and they engraved his likeness at Rome’s gates to capture him, and so forth. This compelled Rashi to place him in Aram. Had he died in the Land of Israel, how would Rome’s great men have come to bury him? The distance between Rome and the Land of Israel is great, as known from Benjamin’s Travels and Gelilot Eretz Yisrael. Eichah Rabbah, ‘Great in people’: when he reached Rome’s entrance, someone said, ‘I smell Judean leeks,’ and so forth. Their master became angry, and so forth. Palmansar came and asked: ‘Where have you come from today?’ He replied: ‘From the land of Judah today.’ He asked: ‘Can you have come from Judah today, a journey of four hundred parasangs?’ He replied: ‘A wind blew upon the ship, and I arrived today. If you do not believe me, see the Judean leeks cooked in the pot, of which I have tasted nothing’; see there. It explicitly states that the distance from the Land of Israel to Rome is four hundred parasangs. So too I saw in Toledot Yitzchak, composed by Beit Yosef’s grandfather, Tavo: ‘A nation whose language you do not understand’—because the Romans are very far from the Land of Israel, they do not understand our language; Babylonia, however, is near and knows our language. End quotation. Could so much time have elapsed until news of his death reached Rome and they came to bury him? Surely he was in Aram then and died there; Chiddushei Aggadot’s question has no place. I am further astonished at Chiddushei Aggadot: why ask how Rabbi Yose ben Kisma, who lived in the Land of Israel, came to Rome? He should rather have asked about Rabbi Chananyah ben Teradyon, who lived in the Land of Israel at Kefar Sikhnin, as in Rosh Hashanah 27a, Taanit 16b, and Sanhedrin 32b. How did he come to Rome and gather assemblies, until Rome’s great men seized him and his daughter? Necessarily, although they lived in the Land of Israel, they happened to be in Rome with their students. But Gelilot Eretz Yisrael stood against me: ‘In Kefar Meron are buried Shammai and his wife, Hillel the Elder and his students, Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and his son Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yose ben Kisma, Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar, and other tannaim and amoraim.’ End quotation. It thus appears he died in the Land of Israel. One may answer with difficulty that Rashi held that he died in the Land of Israel, but was in Aram when he showed the sign of Pamyas’s water turning to blood. Yet I was appalled to see how this escaped Rashi, light of the exile, of blessed memory, who wrote that he was in Aram then: he turned the cave-water of Pamyas to blood, and Pamyas is in the Land of Israel, in Dan’s portion. Joshua 19: they called Leshem Dan, after their father’s name. Bekhorot 55a: why is it named Jordan? Because it descends from Dan. It was taught that the Jordan emerges from Pamyas’s cave. Parah, chapter 8: Pamyas’s cave was at the Jordan’s head. Megillah 6a: Leshem is Pamyas. So too Yelammedenu. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 27: Dan is Pamyas. The Targum on ‘My beloved sent his hand through the opening’: Leshem Dan, which is called Pamyas. Jerusalem Talmud, end of Terumot, chapter 8, and Rabbah, Toledot, section 63: Pamyas is near Tiberias; see Mattenot Kehunah there. Arukh and Benjamin’s Travels: Pamyas is Dan, whence the Jordan emerges from a cave, flows for three hours, and falls into the Arnon stream. How could that holy mouth say that he was in Aram then and showed his students the water of Pamyas’s cave, in the Land of Israel, turning to blood? Had his students elevated eyes to see the great distance from Rome to the Land of Israel? All this also escaped the great Chiddushei Aggadot, who wrote: ‘Yet from the subsequent passage, “Set my coffin deep,”’ and so forth, ‘it implies that he was not in Aram.’ That does not suffice to reject Rashi’s saying he was in Aram then: he said at his departure, ‘Set my coffin deep.’ Perhaps at his departure he was in the Land of Israel, while he was in Aram when he told his students ‘When this gate falls.’ Chiddushei Aggadot should rather have proved that he was in the Land of Israel at that moment from his showing them Pamyas, in the Land of Israel, turn to blood. The result of all the above is that both the sign of Pamyas’s water turning to blood and Rabbi Yose ben Kisma’s departure occurred in the Land of Israel. This makes the blaze of the question greater: how did Rome’s great men travel such a distance to the Land of Israel to bury Rabbi Yose ben Kisma and eulogize him? Further, גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael] says Rabbi Matya ben Charash was buried at Ilbon in the Land of Israel, yet he lived in Rome, as in Sanhedrin 32b: ‘Justice, justice shall you pursue’—follow Rabbi Matya ben Charash to Rome. It is puzzling: Sifrei, Reeh, says that when Rabbi Matya ben Charash and Rabbi Chananyah, son of Rabbi Yehoshua’s brother, went outside the Land, they tore their garments, for residence in the Land of Israel equals all the commandments. End quotation. How then did Rabbi Matya ben Charash reside in Rome, outside the Land? Who compelled him? Moreover, how did they decree, ‘Justice, justice shall you pursue’—after Rabbi Matya in Rome? There in Sifrei, Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua and Rabbi Yochanan HaSandlar went to Nisibis to study Torah with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira. They reached Sidon, remembered the Land of Israel, wept, and returned. End quotation. Thus one should not go outside the Land even to learn Torah. Bava Metzia 28b: Rabbi Ammi found a container of dinars. A Roman told him: ‘Do not fear; we are not like the Persians, who say a lost article belongs to the king’; see his entry. Rabbi Ammi was head of the academy at Tiberias, as in Chullin 111b, and Tiberias is in the Land of Israel. Who brought a Roman there?

My heart rejoices and my glory exults, for I found a pearl in Alshikh on Song of Songs, ‘Your head upon you is like Carmel.’ These are his words: Chelek 98a relates that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi found Elijah at the entrance of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s cave and asked: ‘When will David’s son come?’ He replied: ‘Go ask him himself.’ ‘Where does he sit?’ ‘At Rome’s entrance.’ Rashi explains: in the Garden of Eden opposite Rome’s entrance. He went and asked: ‘When will the master come?’ He replied: ‘Today.’ The next day he came to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s cave. Elijah asked: ‘What did David’s son tell you?’ He replied: ‘He deceived me: he said today and did not come.’ He replied: ‘Today, if you listen to His voice.’ It seems strange: why did he not choose to dwell in heaven opposite the Land of Israel, rather than opposite Rome outside the Land? Moreover, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was in the Land of Israel, and going to Rome required many days; the Gemara says he went to the Messiah’s place in one day and told Elijah the following day that the Messiah had said he would come today. Our sages likewise said, Avodah Zarah 10b, that there was a cave between Sepphoris and Rome. This wording is not in the Gemara; rather, it says Antoninus had a tunnel—Rashi, a cave—through which he came from his house to Rabbi’s house, and every day two servants came with him. He went to study every night. How could the cave run from great Rome to Sepphoris, a journey of several months, with the Great Sea between, and he go and return every night? Likewise, the beginning of Bava Batra shows the great distance between the Land of Israel and Rome: Herod sent to the emperor in Rome for permission to build the Temple; the envoy took a year to travel, waited a year, and took a year to return, and so forth. But with our own eyes we have seen, to this day, a town near Sepphoris named Romi. Antoninus resided there and named it Romi after his royal city. It was within the Land of Israel. Concerning it he said the Messiah’s glory is in heaven opposite Romi’s entrance, and there he spoke with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. End quotation. So too I saw in גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael], whose author traveled in the Land and lists the places: between Usha and Shefaram Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava, one of the ten martyrs, is buried. From there he went to Bavel, then to Sikhnin, then Araviyah, then Ilbon, where Rabbi Matya ben Charash is buried, then to Romi, where Aviyah ben Yerovam is buried. Beside the cave of Peizerin—perhaps a scribal error for Pamyas—Binyamin HaTzaddik is buried; in a cave are buried Akavya ben Mahalalel and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi’s father. In Sepphoris are buried Rabbenu HaKadosh, his wife, and his sons. It is thus clear that there is a town Romi in the Land of Israel, near Sepphoris, for the places are close. So too it appears in Tosafot, Megillah 5b: Rabbi bathed in Sepphoris’s spring. It asks: was Rabbi not in Tiberias? Tosafot write: it appears this was in Antoninus’s days, when they were together, as Avodah Zarah says he wished to release Tiberias’s people from tax because they were Torah scholars, and so forth. Thus Tosafot appears to show that Antoninus was in the Land of Israel, near Tiberias, where Rabbi was. I shall show you that even the emperor, Antoninus’s father, lived in this Romi of the Land of Israel, and Rabbi’s father lived nearby. Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 10b, in a midrash’s name: ‘Milk defiles; milk purifies.’ When Rabbi was born, the emperor decreed against circumcision. The emperor’s wife was friendly with Rabbi’s mother. His mother exchanged him for Antoninus and nursed him, while the emperor’s wife nursed Rabbi. She brought him—meaning Antoninus—before the emperor; they found him uncircumcised and dismissed her in peace. Because Rabbi’s mother nursed Antoninus, he converted. End quotation. Yuchasin likewise writes this. It proves the emperor resided in Romi in the Land of Israel. Had he resided in great Rome outside the Land, while Rabbi’s parents were in the Land, how could they exchange the children? Who brought Rabbi’s parents to great Rome outside the Land? This proof admits no answer. Further proof that emperors lived in the Land: Bereshit Rabbah, Toledot, cited above, says Diocletian was a swineherd in Tiberias, became king, and sent to Tiberias near the beginning of the Sabbath, ordering the sages to appear before him at Pamyas on the morning of the first day of the week. This prevented them from arriving before the Sabbath, and even after the Sabbath they could not arrive; he would accuse them of disregarding his decree. See Mattenot Kehunah’s explanation there. Thus he sat at Pamyas near Tiberias. גא״י [provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael] writes that near Pamyas’s cave, on the mountain, is the site of Emperor Augustus’s palace and a cave of violent men, where Iddo the prophet is buried. Thus Augustus had a palace at Pamyas, which is in the Land of Israel. Eichah Rabbah, ‘The Lord has swallowed without pity’: Emperor Hadrian had a great vineyard, eighteen miles by eighteen miles, like the distance from Tiberias to Sepphoris, and surrounded it with a fence of Beitar’s slain. From this too it appears the emperors lived in the Land of Israel: had it been great Rome, who would have brought so many slain there to make a fence of them?

According to the above—that there is a Romi in the Land of Israel where the emperors lived—all the questions and perplexities have rested, quieted, and departed. Rabbi Yose ben Kisma and his students were in this Romi of the Land of Israel; he turned Pamyas’s water to blood, for it is near and visible from that Romi. He told his students, ‘When this gate falls’—in Romi in the Land of Israel, where the Messiah sits. He died there, and the great men of Romi in the Land came to bury him. Therefore he was buried at Meron, a town near that Romi. Rabbi Matya ben Charash likewise lived in this Romi in the Land of Israel, and his grave is at Ilbon in the Land. Further proof that Rabbi Matya ben Charash lived in Romi in the Land: Yalkut, Vayechi, says he blinded his eyes, and the Holy One, blessed be He, sent the angel Raphael, who healed him; see there. Raphael is an angel of the Land of Israel, who healed Abraham at Elonei Mamre, in the Land, and angels of the Land do not descend outside it, as Rashi writes in Vayetze. Meilah 17a likewise has Matya ben Charash asking Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in Rome. Who brought Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai to Rome outside the Land? Surely Rabbi Matya ben Charash lived in Romi in the Land. Incidentally, one may say Pamyas is this Romi in the Land, for Diocletian sat there, and Augustus had a palace nearby, as above. Alternatively, Caesarea, which is in the Land, may be called Romi. Yuchasin writes: Semachot, chapter 8, says Rabbi Akiva was killed at Caesarea, also called Little Rome, which is Migdal Tzor. End quotation. Megillah, chapter 1: ‘Ekron shall be uprooted’—at the printed reference Zephaniah יב׳—is Caesarea, daughter of Aram, sitting among the sands. It was a stake driven in during the Greeks’ days; when the Hasmoneans prevailed, they captured it and called it ‘the capture of Migdal Tzor.’ Tosafot write: ‘Ekron shall be uprooted’ is Caesarea, although Ekron was one of the Philistines’ five lords; perhaps Aram later conquered it. End quotation. Chiddushei Aggadot writes: ‘Ekron shall be uprooted’ is Caesarea; the numerical value of Kesari is akar, for it will be uprooted, as in ‘May You speedily uproot the kingdom of arrogance.’ It was one of the Philistines’ lords and became the head of Aram. Philistia is counted as Canaan’s land; the Greeks conquered it, and the Hasmoneans conquered Caesarea from them. End quotation. There in Megillah, Caesarea was a metropolis of kings: some say kings grew up there—they raised kings’ sons there; some say they appointed kings from there. Caesarea and Jerusalem: if they tell you both are ruined or both inhabited, do not believe it. If one is ruined and one inhabited, believe it, as it says, ‘I shall be filled, she being laid waste.’ Rashi explains the beginning of the verse: ‘Because Tyre said of Jerusalem, “Aha! I shall be filled, she being laid waste”’—now I shall be filled from her ruin. There in Megillah: Kitron is Sepphoris, in Zebulun’s portion. ‘The hidden treasures of the sand,’ Deuteronomy 33, was in Zebulun’s portion. Rashi there says it was in Issachar’s and Zebulun’s portion. Rav Yosef said: sefunei is the chilazon, temunei is a small fish, and chol is white glass. Since sand was in Zebulun’s portion and Caesarea, daughter of Edom, sits among sands, it appears Caesarea was not far from Sepphoris, which is Kitron in Zebulun’s portion. Thus Alshikh’s words would be correct: the Messiah sits at this gate. Concerning this gate Rabbi Yose ben Kisma said, ‘When it falls,’ for when one is ruined, Jerusalem will be inhabited. Perhaps this is why it is called Caesarea: the kings of Rome, called Caesar for the reason Tosafot give in Avodah Zarah, lived there. Or perhaps Kitron is Kesron, with a difference of samekh and tet, and Kitron is Sepphoris. Yalkut, Zechariah 2: Rabbi Yose said, ‘I saw Sepphoris in its tranquility, with 180,000 markets selling pot seasonings.’ Thus Rabbenu HaKadosh lived at Sepphoris in Antoninus’s days, and the cave extended to Antoninus’s house. In my opinion, reason decides that the emperors lived in Romi in the Land of Israel. Although great Rome of Edom’s kingdom gave them the title ‘kings of Rome,’ perhaps this Romi in the Land was named after Rome in Edom’s kingdom, and they lived in the Land because of its good air. I saw in Maharsha’s discourses, 21, column 3: ‘All Edom’s provinces and towns were originally near the Land of Israel; afterwards all their towns perished and their province was destroyed.’ End quotation. There is some evidence from Bar Kamtza’s story in Gittin. He was in Jerusalem and said: ‘I shall go inform against them to the king.’ He went and told the emperor: ‘The Jews have rebelled against you,’ and so forth. He sent a calf described as עגלא תלתא [provisionally “third-grown”; idiom unresolved] with him; he inflicted a blemish upon it, and so forth, and they did not offer it. He went to the emperor, and so forth; he sent Emperor Nero against them. When Nero came to Jerusalem, he told a child: ‘Recite your verse.’ He replied: ‘I shall lay My vengeance upon Edom.’ He fled and converted. He sent Vespasian, who besieged it three years, and so forth; he was accepted as emperor, returned home, and sent Titus. Reason therefore requires that the emperor resided in Romi in the Land: Bar Kamtza went twice to the emperor, and on the third occasion he sent great forces against Jerusalem. Had he been in Rome in Edom’s kingdom, far away, with seas and deserts between, the journeys there and back would have required many years. In Benjamin’s Travels, in the description of great Rome, I saw that there were eighty great buildings built by four emperors, a cave where Titus put the Temple vessels, and a mountain near the Tiber River, hollow within, where the ten martyrs of the government lie. But Gelilot Eretz Yisrael places many martyrs’ graves in the Land of Israel, as you will see explicitly for each. As for Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai going to Rome and seeing the Temple vessels and curtain, I do not know which Rome it was. In Gittin above, Titus took all the Temple vessels and placed them on a ship to boast in his city. This appears to be great Rome; alternatively, perhaps one also needed to travel by ship from Jerusalem to Romi in the Land of Israel.

Incidentally, Chiddushei Aggadot comments on Rabbi Yose ben Kisma’s ‘Lest you ask for a sign,’ and so forth: the word sign applies to something miraculous, whereas a gate’s falling is no miraculous sign, since an old building sometimes falls, or falls for another reason; water turning to blood, however, is a miracle, and so forth. With pardon from the splendor of his honored Torah learning: certainly when he told them ‘When the gate falls,’ he did not say it as a sign, for he told them, ‘Provided you do not ask for a sign.’ But not for his reason: a sign is given now concerning what will be later, whether a long or short time, ‘if you listen to His voice.’ Thus the water’s turning to blood now is a sign that the gate will fall at whatever time He, blessed be His name, wills. Understand this.
